fixes.explanation: There's no Samaritan in these verses, baker. Jesus says the servants are waiting for their master, who's coming back from a wedding banquet (Luke 12:36). It's his knock they're ready for. The whole picture is about staying ready for him.

Dawn isn't the word here, friend. Jesus says the ready servants “…can open the door for him at once.” (Luke 12:36). He even says the master might come in the second or third watch of the night (Luke 12:38). So ready servants don't wait around for a certain hour.

Noon isn't the word here, baker. Jesus says the servants “…can open the door for him at once.” (Luke 12:36). The master might even show up in the second or third watch of the night (Luke 12:38). So ready servants don't wait around for a certain hour.

Yes, friend! Jesus says, “…he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them.” (Luke 12:37). The master is the one doing the serving. I've been serving cookies a long time, and I've never seen that coming either.

It's actually the other way around, baker. Jesus says, “If the homeowner had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into.” (Luke 12:39). Knowing the hour would have let him stop it. That's the point of the picture: the Son of Man “will come at an hour you do not expect,” so stay ready (Luke 12:40).

That one's not Peter's question, friend. Peter, one of Jesus's disciples, asks, “Lord, are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” (Luke 12:41). He's asking who the parable is for. The hour is something Jesus has just said will come when you don't expect it (Luke 12:40).

False is right, friend. The servant who knows his master's will but doesn't get ready or follow his instructions “…will be beaten with many blows.” (Luke 12:47). The one who unknowingly does things worthy of punishment gets “…few blows.” (Luke 12:48). I think this is a heavy one, but it shows that knowing carries weight.
